title: Sudden tearing chest pain and a blackout in a 66-year-old man
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and examination of a 66-year-old man brought to the ED by ambulance with sudden, tearing central chest pain through to his back, a brief blackout and breathlessness. He becomes hypotensive during the station. The candidate then interprets his observations, ECG, bloods and CT aortogram, recognises a Stanford type A aortic dissection, and outlines emergency management and safety netting.
focus: Acute chest pain: a cluster-question history that recognises aortic dissection, a bedside search for its signs, and emergency surgical management without antithrombotics
stem:
You are the junior doctor in the Emergency Department of a tertiary hospital that has a cardiothoracic surgical unit on site. Giuseppe, a 66-year-old retired bricklayer, has been brought in by ambulance with chest pain. He is on a trolley in the acute area on a cardiac monitor, with an IV cannula in place.

A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Giuseppe and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Act on anything the nurse tells you (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Giuseppe's observations, his 12-lead ECG, his blood results and his CT aortogram report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Giuseppe, a 66-year-old retired bricklayer. You are lying propped up on the trolley, pale and sweaty, and you cannot get comfortable. You are in the worst pain of your life. You talk in short sentences and keep pressing on your chest. You are frightened. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they examine.

Opening line: "It's like something's ripping inside my chest... it goes right through to my back."

History (give only when asked)

The pain

  • Site: the middle of your chest.
  • Onset: about an hour and a half ago at home, all of a sudden. It was at its worst from the very first second.
  • Character: excruciating and tearing, "like something is ripping".
  • Radiation: straight through to your back.
  • Time course: steady and unchanged since it started.
  • Exacerbating and relieving factors: nothing makes it better or worse, including position and breathing. The injection from the ambulance barely touched it.
  • Severity: 10/10, the worst pain you have ever had.
  • Before: you have never had this pain before.
  • Impact: you could not do anything. Your wife called the ambulance and you came straight to hospital.

Associated symptoms

  • Dizziness: yes, since the pain started.
  • Blackout: yes. Soon after the pain started you blacked out completely. Your wife says it was less than a minute and you came round quickly. If asked: you were sitting, so you did not hit your head; your wife saw no jerking; you did not wet yourself or bite your tongue; you were not confused afterwards.
  • Breathlessness: yes, you have been short of breath since it started.
  • If asked about other symptoms (say no): no weakness or numbness in your arms, legs or face; no trouble speaking or seeing; no belly pain; no pain, coldness or numbness in your legs.

Other causes (all negative, give only if asked)

  • Heart attack: the pain is not crushing or squeezing and does not go to your jaw or arms. No vomiting. You are sweaty now.
  • Clots: no calf pain or swelling, no long trips or flights, no recent operation or time in bed, no previous clots, no cancer that you know of, no coughing up blood, no racing heart.
  • Collapsed lung: no injury or fall, the pain is not worse on breathing in, no lung disease.
  • Pericarditis: no recent cold or flu, no fever, the pain is no better leaning forward.
  • Heart failure or valve disease: no breathlessness lying flat, no waking at night gasping, no ankle swelling, no breathlessness or fainting on exertion before today.
  • Gut and chest wall: no reflux, indigestion or burping, no injury, the chest is not tender to touch.
  • Anxiety: no panic attacks, no anxious mood before today.
  • Connective tissue: nobody has ever said you have Marfan or a "stretchy" condition. No diabetes.

Past medical history

  • High blood pressure for years.
  • High cholesterol.
  • Enlarged prostate: once you could not pass urine and needed a catheter.
  • Osteoarthritis in your foot.
  • No previous heart problems, no heart tests, no operations on the heart or aorta.

Medications

  • Perindopril 5 mg daily, verapamil SR 180 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg at night.
  • Over the counter: paracetamol or ibuprofen for the foot pain.
  • No blood thinners or aspirin. No vitamins or supplements. No recreational drugs.

Allergies: none.

Family history

  • Mother: died of "old age".
  • Father: died suddenly at 65. You cannot remember clearly, but the doctors said it was his heart.
  • Sister (60): also has high blood pressure.

Social history

  • Smoking: half a pack a day since you were 23, and you still smoke.
  • Alcohol: a glass of red wine with dinner on weeknights.
  • Retired bricklayer. You walk to the grocery store or the park every day.
  • Your wife Maria cooks homemade Italian food.
  • No recent travel.
  • You live with Maria. Your sons and daughter live nearby with their own families and visit often. Maria is following the ambulance by car.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think you are having a heart attack, the first time this has ever happened. You are worried you will not make it, like your father. You want them to stop the pain and fix it.

  • If the candidate has not asked by about minute 4, say: "Is it a heart attack, doctor? My father died of his heart at my age."

The nurse and how Giuseppe changes

  • When asked, the nurse gives the arrival observations (10:12): HR 98 regular, BP 150/88 (left arm), RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C, BGL 7.2 mmol/L. The paramedics gave 50 micrograms of IV fentanyl, which barely helped. They held the aspirin because the pain went through to his back. No GTN was given.
  • If the candidate asks for an ECG, the nurse says it was recorded at 10:15 and the examiner will give it in Part 2. Bloods were sent from the cannula at 10:18.
  • If the candidate asks for a CT, the nurse says the ED consultant has requested an urgent CT aortogram; the report will be given in Part 2. If they ask for a bedside echo before the BP falls, the nurse says the consultant has been asked to do one urgently. If they ask for a bedside echo after the BP falls, the nurse says the consultant is coming now to do it.
  • If the candidate orders IV opioid analgesia, the nurse gives it. By the end of Part 1 the pain eases a little, to 7/10, but never goes.
  • If the candidate orders any other medicine (including aspirin, heparin, GTN or a beta blocker), the nurse says "I'll draw it up." The examiner notes it for marking. Apart from opioid analgesia, nothing ordered had been given when the BP fell. A BP-lowering drug ordered before the fall is not given unless the candidate confirms it after the fall; the nurse does not prompt.
  • About 7 minutes into Part 1 (or as the examination begins, if sooner), the nurse says: "Doctor, he says he feels faint again. He's grey and clammy. BP is 96 over 60 in the left arm and his heart rate is 112." Giuseppe says: "I feel like I'm going to pass out again."
  • If the candidate lies him flat, he feels slightly less faint, but the BP stays about 96/60 and he stays pale and clammy.

Exam findings

  • General: pale, sweaty, distressed and restless, speaking in short sentences. Alert. Not tall or thin, normal arm span, no high-arched palate, no long fingers: no Marfanoid features.
  • Pulses: right radial pulse weaker than the left. Rate 98 and regular (112 after the nurse's report). Femoral pulses palpable and equal.
  • Blood pressure: left arm 150/88, right arm 118/72. After the nurse's report: left arm 96/60, right arm 72/48.
  • Perfusion: cool hands, CRT 3 seconds (4 seconds after the nurse's report).
  • JVP: 3 cm above the sternal angle. After the nurse's report: 6 cm above the sternal angle; pulsus paradoxus about 14 mmHg if the candidate asks for it.
  • Heart: apex not displaced. Dual heart sounds. A soft, blowing early diastolic murmur at the right and left sternal edges, loudest at the right sternal edge sitting forward in held expiration. No pericardial rub. After the nurse's report: heart sounds softer.
  • Chest: RR 20 (26 after the nurse's report). Trachea central, expansion equal, resonant to percussion, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze.
  • Chest wall: not tender.
  • Neurological: GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, no facial droop, normal speech, normal power and sensation in all four limbs.
  • Abdomen: soft and non-tender, no pulsatile mass, bladder not palpable.
  • Legs: warm, femoral, popliteal and foot pulses present and equal. Calves soft and non-tender, no swelling.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Giuseppe's identity and explains what they are doing while he is in severe pain.

Recognises a time-critical emergency from the start: confirms continuous cardiac monitoring is running, asks the nurse for the observations and a 12-lead ECG, and keeps the history short and targeted.
Uses plain language and empathy: acknowledges his pain and his fear that he will not make it, and offers analgesia early.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Site and onset: central chest, sudden, at full intensity from the start
Character and severity: excruciating and tearing, 10/10, unchanged since onset
No relieving or exacerbating factors, a first episode, and its impact (could do nothing, ambulance straight to ED)

check.d: Critical needs sudden onset at maximal intensity, tearing or severe character, and radiation to the back. Other features supporting.

check.x: Asks about dizziness and breathlessness, and characterises the blackout: witnessed, under 1 minute, quick recovery, no head injury, no jerking, incontinence or tongue biting.
check.d: Critical needs the blackout identified and characterised as syncope (witnessed, duration, quick recovery, plus at least one of no jerking, incontinence or tongue biting) and breathlessness asked. Other features supporting.

check.x: Asks about symptoms of branch-vessel malperfusion: limb or facial weakness or numbness, speech or vision change, abdominal pain, and leg pain, coldness or numbness.
check.d: Critical needs neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness, speech or vision) plus at least one of abdominal pain or leg pain, coldness or numbness.

check.x: Asks focused questions to weigh at least three other causes (e.g. MI: crushing pain or jaw/arm radiation; PE: calf symptoms, immobility, previous clot; pneumothorax/pericarditis: pleuritic or positional pain, recent viral illness).
check.d: Credit any three of myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax, pericarditis, and heart failure or aortic stenosis.

check.x: Past history and risk factors: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, smoking (still smoking, about 21 pack-years), connective tissue disease, previous heart/aortic disease; BPH with previous retention.
Takes the medication and allergy history:
check.d: Critical needs regular medications asked (including the BP drugs), a specific question about blood thinners or antiplatelets, and allergies. Credit OTC analgesics, statin and supplements as supporting.

kids.x: Perindopril, verapamil and atorvastatin, with over-the-counter paracetamol and ibuprofen for the foot
No anticoagulants, antiplatelets or supplements, and no allergies

check.x: Asks about a family history of sudden death or aortic disease: father died suddenly at 65 "of his heart".
Brief social history: who is at home and next of kin (wife Maria, on her way), alcohol.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: he thinks it is a heart attack and is frightened he will not make it, like his father.
Examination
General inspection and vital signs: pale, sweaty, distressed; looks for Marfanoid features.

Compares both radial pulses and the BP in both arms, and identifies the weaker right radial pulse and a systolic difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms (left 150/88 vs right 118/72 before the fall, or left 96/60 vs right 72/48 after it).

Cardiovascular examination: perfusion (CRT, peripheries), JVP, heart sounds, a pericardial rub, and identifies the early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation at the right or left sternal edge (either is accepted).
Respiratory examination: trachea, expansion, percussion and auscultation, looking for a pneumothorax, effusion or crackles.
Brief neurological screen for malperfusion: conscious state, pupils, face, speech, and limb power and sensation.
Examines the abdomen (tenderness, pulsatile mass, bladder) and the legs (femoral and foot pulses, calves).

Responds to the nurse's report of BP 96/60 and HR 112: recognises the deterioration, reassesses ABC at once, calls the ED senior/consultant to the bedside now and moves him to resus (or a rapid response/MET call per local ED policy), and gives no BP-lowering drugs, cancelling any beta blocker, GTN or other antihypertensive ordered before the fall.
check.d: The critical mark needs only these four elements. Also credit, as supporting elements: positions him flat or as tolerated, second large-bore cannula, crossmatch, reassesses JVP and heart sounds, requests urgent bedside echo for tamponade. A candidate who ordered a BP-lowering drug before the fall earns the critical mark only if they cancel it after the nurse's report.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the observations: normal-zone values on arrival despite a 32 mmHg arm difference; at 10:24 yellow-zone SBP 96, RR 26 and SpO2 94% with HR 112 means early shock needing the ED senior at the bedside now.
States there is no ST elevation, so no STEMI, and that the lateral changes are long-standing LVH strain (unchanged from 2024), not acute ischaemia.
Notes first-degree AV block (relevant to beta blockade on verapamil) and LVH with strain.

Interprets the bloods: lactate 2.8 with low bicarbonate means hypoperfusion; the mild troponin rise is not primary ACS and is not a reason for antithrombotics; coagulation normal and group and screen done for theatre.
check.d: Also credit: Hb 128 may underestimate blood loss; D-dimer markedly raised but adds little at ADD-RS ≥2; troponin may be demand or coronary ostial involvement (ostia not assessable on non-gated CT).

check.x: Interprets the CT aortogram: an intimal flap in the ascending aorta, so Stanford type A, with haemopericardium and possible early tamponade.
check.d: Critical needs type A and haemopericardium/tamponade. Also credit, as supporting: extent to the infrarenal aorta, brachiocephalic trunk involvement explaining the weak right radial and lower right arm BP, dilated root, perfused visceral and renal arteries, DeBakey I.

check.x: Gives acute Stanford type A aortic dissection as the diagnosis, justified from the history (sudden tearing pain to the back, syncope, hypertension, smoking), the examination (arm BP difference, pulse deficit, aortic regurgitation murmur) and the CT.
Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against: myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, pneumothorax and pericarditis.
Management

Resuscitates in the resus bay: senior ED doctor at the bedside, continuous monitoring, two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch with the blood bank alerted (massive transfusion protocol on standby), and BP measured in the higher (left) arm, or by a left radial arterial line (the right under-reads because of brachiocephalic involvement).
check.d: Critical needs resus/senior at the bedside, two large-bore cannulas and crossmatch with the blood bank alerted. Supporting: MTP on standby, and BP in the left arm or by a left radial arterial line with the reason.

check.x: Calls the cardiothoracic surgical team now for emergency surgery, with cardiac anaesthesia and ICU, and does not delay theatre for further tests.

Manages the hypotension: no BP-lowering drugs now; fluid or blood in small volumes titrated to conscious state and perfusion; recognises possible tamponade and states that surgery, not routine pericardiocentesis, is the treatment.

States BP lowering and beta blockade are withheld now (hypotension, tamponade); if hypertension returns, IV beta blocker first (HR about 60, SBP 100–120 mmHg), vasodilator only after, with CTS/ICU input, cautious with verapamil and first-degree AV block.
Gives titrated IV opioid analgesia (for example fentanyl in small increments) with an antiemetic, watching the BP.
Does not give aspirin, heparin, thrombolysis or other antithrombotics, and states why (bleeding from the aorta or into the pericardium, and urgent surgery).
check.d: Fail if aspirin, heparin or thrombolysis was ordered in Part 1 and not withdrawn once dissection was considered.

check.x: Withholds his oral medicines (perindopril, verapamil, ibuprofen), keeps him fasted for theatre, and plans a urinary catheter for hourly urine output, aware of his previous urinary retention.
Safety netting

Explains in plain language that this is a tear in the wall of the main artery, not a heart attack, that it needs an urgent operation, is honest that it is serious, checks understanding, tells him the surgeon will explain the operation and take consent, and offers to call his wife Maria.
check.d: Needs not a heart attack, torn main artery, urgent operation and honesty; checking understanding, consent by the surgeon and calling Maria are supporting.

check.x: Keeps him on continuous monitoring with a nurse at the bedside and names triggers for immediate escalation to the ED consultant and CTS registrar: further fall in BP, change in pain, new neurological signs, abdominal or leg pain.
check.d: Critical needs continuous monitoring plus at least three named triggers.

check.x: Tells Giuseppe in plain words to tell the nurse straight away if the pain gets worse or moves, he feels faint, more breathless, has weakness, numbness or trouble speaking, or belly or leg pain.

part2.lead: Here are Giuseppe's observations from arrival, his 12-lead ECG, his blood results and the CT aortogram report. ED consultant bedside echo 10:28: moderate pericardial effusion with early right atrial diastolic collapse, dilated aortic root with a possible flap, aortic regurgitation; CTS registrar aware, agreed to immediate CT en route to theatre as he was maintaining BP about 96/60.
part2.patient:
Ask this straight after the examiner reads question 4. The candidate answers you directly as part of question 4.

  • "Was it a heart attack? Am I going to make it?"
  • If they mention an operation: "Can someone call my wife Maria?"

You are very frightened. You settle a little if the candidate explains clearly, without jargon, and is honest but kind. If they say "dissection" without explaining it, ask: "What does that mean?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. BP taken in the left arm (right arm 118/72 at 10:12 and 72/48 at 10:24). The 10:24 set was taken when Giuseppe said he felt faint again; any medicine other than analgesia ordered in Part 1 had not been given. Pain score at 10:24 recorded before any further analgesia.
handover.model:
• Read: at 10:12 every value is in the white zone (RR 20, SpO2 96% RA, BP 150/88, HR 98, temperature 36.6 °C, alert), but pain is 10/10, CRT 3 seconds, and the right arm reads 32 mmHg lower. At 10:24 systolic 96, RR 26 and SpO2 94% are in the yellow zone; HR 112 is white; CRT 4 seconds; the nurse is concerned.
  • Meaning: a white zone chart did not make him safe. He is now in early shock (shock index about 1.2). In suspected dissection this points to haemopericardium with tamponade, rupture, acute aortic regurgitation or coronary involvement. The right arm under-reads because of branch-vessel involvement, so the higher (left) arm is used.
  • Changes: yellow zone values call for a clinical review at least; several yellow values with a worried nurse in the ED means calling the ED senior/consultant to the bedside now and moving him to resus (or a rapid response/MET call per local ED policy). No BP-lowering drugs; crossmatch and theatre.

rows.note: Arrived by ambulance 10:05; fentanyl 50 microgram IV by paramedics; ECG 10:15
Feels faint again, grey and clammy; doctor informed

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG: Giuseppe, 66-year-old man, recorded 10:15 in the ED (25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV).

  • Rate: 98/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm, regular, a P wave before every QRS.
  • Axis: normal, about 0°.
  • PR interval: 216 ms (first-degree AV block).
  • QRS: 96 ms. S in V1 plus R in V5 = 40 mm (LVH by voltage criteria). No pathological Q waves, no bundle branch block.
  • QTc: 440 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: 0.5 to 1 mm downsloping ST depression with asymmetric T wave inversion in I, aVL, V5 and V6. No ST elevation in any lead, including aVR, II, III and aVF.
  • Comparison: GP ECG from 2024: sinus rhythm 70/min, PR 204 ms, the same LVH voltage and the same lateral ST and T wave changes.
handover.model:
• Read: sinus rhythm 98/min, normal axis, first-degree AV block (PR 216 ms), LVH by voltage with lateral ST depression and asymmetric T inversion (a strain pattern), no ST elevation, unchanged from 2024.
  • Meaning: no STEMI; the lateral changes are long-standing hypertensive LVH strain, not acute ischaemia, with AV nodal slowing on verapamil.
  • Changes: no STEMI pathway and no antithrombotics. The AV block means any IV beta blocker on top of verapamil is given cautiously with senior or ICU input. Repeat if the pain or rhythm changes (new ST elevation could mean coronary involvement by the dissection).

handover.label: Bloods and venous gas
handover.result: Venous bloods collected 10:18 from the IV cannula; venous gas at 10:26, after the fall in BP. Group and screen sent; crossmatch on request.
handover.model:
• Read: Hb 128, mildly low (an early Hb underestimates acute blood loss; repeat after the fall in BP); WCC 11.8 with neutrophilia (stress). Creatinine 108 against a baseline of 94, eGFR 65. hs-troponin T 24, mildly raised. D-dimer 6.8, markedly raised. Coagulation normal. pH low-normal (7.33) with bicarbonate 20, base excess -5 and lactate 2.8: a mild lactic metabolic acidosis, compensated so far. Group O positive, antibody screen negative.
  • Meaning: hypoperfusion and possible blood loss (into the pericardium). With ADD-RS ≥2 the D-dimer adds little: it is non-specific (also raised in PE) and a normal result would not have excluded dissection. The small troponin rise (taken before the BP fell) may be demand (LVH, tachycardia, pain) or coronary involvement by the dissection, which the non-gated CT cannot exclude; it is not primary ACS and is not a reason for antithrombotics. Normal coagulation and a negative antibody screen mean blood is quickly available for theatre.
  • Changes: crossmatch now and alert the blood bank; repeat the gas, Hb and lactate; recheck renal function and watch urine output.

handover.label: CT aortogram
handover.result:
Examination: CT aortogram, chest, abdomen and pelvis: non-contrast then arterial phase IV contrast, 10:38. Non-ECG-gated.

Clinical details: 66-year-old man with sudden tearing central chest pain radiating to the back, syncope, arm BP difference, now hypotensive. ?Aortic dissection.

Findings:

  • Aortic root and ascending aorta: aortic root 46 mm, ascending aorta 52 mm. An intimal flap arises in the ascending aorta just above the sinotubular junction. The coronary ostia cannot be assessed reliably on this non-gated study.
  • Arch and branches: the flap extends through the arch and into the brachiocephalic trunk, which is narrowed by false lumen. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise from the true lumen and enhance normally.
  • Descending and abdominal aorta: the dissection continues through the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta, ending in the infrarenal aorta above the bifurcation. The coeliac axis, superior mesenteric artery and both renal arteries arise from the true lumen and enhance. Both kidneys enhance symmetrically. Iliac and femoral arteries normal.
  • Pericardium: moderate high-attenuation pericardial effusion (haemopericardium), maximum depth 14 mm, with mild flattening of the right atrial wall.
  • Mediastinum: no periaortic contrast extravasation.
  • Lungs and pleura: mild dependent atelectasis. No pneumothorax, no pleural effusion. No large central pulmonary artery filling defect (pulmonary arteries not optimally opacified on arterial phase).
  • Other: prostate enlarged. No acute bony abnormality.

Conclusion: acute Stanford type A (DeBakey type I) aortic dissection from the ascending aorta to the infrarenal abdominal aorta, involving the brachiocephalic trunk, with a dilated aortic root and ascending aorta and a moderate haemopericardium that may indicate early tamponade; correlate with echocardiography. Findings phoned to the ED consultant at 10:46.
handover.model:
• Read: an intimal flap starting in the ascending aorta (type A, DeBakey I) running to the infrarenal aorta, involving the brachiocephalic trunk; root and ascending aorta dilated; visceral and renal arteries from the true lumen and perfused; moderate haemopericardium with right atrial flattening; no extravasation; no pneumothorax.
  • Meaning: confirms the diagnosis and explains every bedside finding: the weak right radial and lower right arm BP (brachiocephalic involvement), the aortic regurgitation murmur (root involvement), and the hypotension, raised JVP and soft heart sounds (haemopericardium, early tamponade, as on the bedside echo). It also argues against pneumothorax and pericarditis.
  • Changes: any type A dissection is a surgical emergency: cardiothoracic surgery now, straight to theatre, with no antithrombotics and no delay for further imaging.

ask: You are now calling the cardiothoracic surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Giuseppe, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Giuseppe now, here in the emergency department.
Giuseppe has a question for you. Please answer him, then tell me how you will keep him safe until he reaches theatre.
expect:
• Identify: self, ED junior doctor; Giuseppe, 66, ED resus.
  • Situation: CT-confirmed acute type A aortic dissection with haemopericardium, now hypotensive: BP 96/60 (left arm), HR 112.
  • Background: sudden tearing chest pain to the back 1.5 h ago, syncope, breathless; hypertension, smoker about 21 pack-years; on verapamil and perindopril; no anticoagulants, no allergies.
  • Assessment: 32 mmHg arm BP difference, weak right radial, aortic regurgitation murmur, raised JVP. Normal zone on arrival, yellow zone at 10:24: early shock. ECG: no STEMI, changes old (LVH strain), first-degree AV block. Bloods: lactate 2.8 with low bicarbonate (hypoperfusion); mild troponin rise, not ACS; coagulation normal, group and screen done. CT: flap in the ascending aorta (type A) with haemopericardium, possible early tamponade.
  • Recommendation: please accept for emergency surgery and review now; I am alerting cardiac anaesthesia, ICU and the blood bank.

Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection with haemopericardium and aortic regurgitation: sudden, maximal tearing pain through to the back, syncope, hypertension and smoking, a pulse deficit and arm BP difference, an early diastolic murmur, very raised D-dimer, and CT confirmation.

  • Myocardial infarction: for: risk factors, father's sudden cardiac death, mild troponin rise; against: tearing pain to the back, no ST elevation, ECG unchanged from 2024.
  • Pulmonary embolism: for: syncope, breathlessness, raised D-dimer; against: no VTE risk factors, normal calves, CT explains the picture.
  • Pneumothorax: against: no trauma, not pleuritic, equal resonance and breath sounds, none on CT.
  • Pericarditis: against: not positional, no viral illness, no rub, no PR depression; the effusion here is blood from the dissection.

1. Resus bay, senior ED doctor at the bedside, continuous monitoring, two large-bore cannulas, BP in the higher (left) arm, or by a left radial arterial line (the right under-reads because of brachiocephalic involvement).
  2. Cardiothoracic surgery now for emergency repair; cardiac anaesthesia and ICU; no delay for further tests.
  3. Hypotensive now: no BP-lowering drugs; small volumes of fluid or blood to maintain conscious state and perfusion; crossmatch, blood bank alerted; surgery, not routine pericardiocentesis, treats the tamponade.
  4. BP lowering and beta blockade withheld now (hypotension, tamponade); if hypertension returns, IV beta blocker first (HR about 60, SBP 100–120 mmHg), vasodilator only after, with CTS/ICU input, cautious with verapamil and first-degree AV block.
  5. Titrated IV opioid with an antiemetic.
  6. No aspirin, heparin or thrombolysis. Withhold oral medicines, fasting, catheter with care (previous retention).

• Plain words: not a heart attack; the wall of the main artery has torn and blood has collected around the heart; he needs an operation now; this is serious, said honestly and kindly; offer to call Maria.
  • Tell the nurse straight away about worse or moving pain, feeling faint, more breathless, weakness, numbness or trouble speaking, or belly or leg pain.
  • Escalation: a nurse stays with him on continuous monitoring, with immediate escalation to the ED consultant and the CTS registrar for a further fall in BP, a change in pain, new neurological signs, or abdominal or leg pain.

ddx.dx: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection
ddx.for: Sudden maximal tearing central pain through to the back with syncope in a hypertensive smoker, a weak right radial with a 32 mmHg arm BP difference, an aortic regurgitation murmur, very raised D-dimer and a CT flap from the ascending aorta.
He is a 66-year-old hypertensive smoker with high cholesterol, his father died suddenly of his heart at 65, and his troponin is mildly raised.
ddx.against: The pain is tearing and goes to the back rather than crushing to the jaw or arm, the ECG shows no ST elevation and is unchanged from 2024, and the small troponin rise can be explained by demand or coronary involvement by the dissection.

ddx.for: He had a blackout with breathlessness, tachycardia and a raised D-dimer.
ddx.against: He has no calf symptoms, travel, immobility, previous clot or cancer, and the arm BP difference, murmur and CT findings explain everything.

ddx.for: He is a smoker with sudden chest pain and breathlessness.
ddx.against: There was no trauma, the pain is not pleuritic, the chest is resonant with equal breath sounds, and CT shows no pneumothorax.

ddx.for: He has central chest pain and a pericardial effusion on CT.
ddx.against: No viral illness or fever, the pain does not change with position, there is no rub or PR depression, and the effusion is high-attenuation blood from the dissection.

guide:
In Part 1, Giuseppe answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine. The nurse gives the arrival observations when asked. About 7 minutes in, or as the examination begins if sooner, the nurse reports BP 96/60 and HR 112, and the later findings apply from then on. The fall in BP happens whatever the candidate has ordered: if they ordered a beta blocker or GTN earlier, say it had not been given. Mark the bedside response (item 22) in Part 1. If the candidate asks for the ECG, bloods or CT, say they will be given in Part 2. Treatment ordered in Part 1 is noted and credited against the Management items in Part 2.

Item 37: a candidate who orders aspirin or heparin in Part 1 before considering dissection earns the item only if they withdraw it once dissection is suspected. Item 17 needs both arms compared and the difference stated. History items: credit focused questions that weigh at least three other causes (item 9) and a past history that covers the risk factors (item 10). Questions about occupation, diet or exercise earn nothing and cost time in a shocked patient.

In Part 2, hand over all four results, then ask the four questions in order, about 90 seconds each (Q4 may be shorter to fit the 5 minutes). Giuseppe's questions come straight after question 4 is read. Credit the type A classification from either the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer; DeBakey I is accepted but not required. Accept esmolol, metoprolol or labetalol for the anti-impulse plan, and accept a systolic target of 100 to 120 mmHg.

A high-performing candidate asks for monitoring and an ECG at once, characterises the pain and the blackout, asks about malperfusion and a few focused questions for the other causes, compares both arms and hears the aortic regurgitation murmur, and acts at once when the BP falls. In Part 2 they read the ECG as having no STEMI with old LVH strain changes, recognise type A from the CT, call cardiothoracic surgery, withhold antithrombotics and BP-lowering drugs while he is hypotensive, and know the anti-impulse targets for when he is not.

A borderline candidate takes a long, unfocused history, does not compare the arms, treats it as ACS with aspirin or heparin, asks for "cardiology review" rather than emergency surgery, lowers the BP despite hypotension, or gives vague safety netting.
explain:
Diagnosis: acute Stanford type A aortic dissection

Giuseppe has sudden, excruciating, tearing central chest pain at full intensity from the start, radiating to the back, with dizziness, a brief blackout and breathlessness. He is a 66-year-old man with hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and a long smoking history. At the bedside he has a pulse deficit, a systolic difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms and an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation. That combination is aortic dissection until proven otherwise. The CT aortogram confirms a flap starting in the ascending aorta (Stanford type A, and DeBakey type I because it starts in the ascending aorta and extends through the arch into the descending aorta; type II would be confined to the ascending aorta), involving the brachiocephalic trunk, with haemopericardium.

With aortic root dilatation (his root is 46 mm), the early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation is often loudest at the right sternal edge rather than the left, which is a useful pointer to aortic root disease rather than primary valve disease.

The history: cardinal features, cluster questions and risk

  • Use the cardinal features (site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, time course, modifying factors, severity) and ask about the effect on daily activities as a measure of severity.
  • Ask cluster questions for each differential rather than a scattergun list: myocardial infarction, dissection, aortic stenosis, pericarditis and heart failure; pneumothorax, PE, pneumonia and lung cancer; GORD; musculoskeletal causes; anxiety.
  • Stratify risk: chest pain in older people is more likely to be cardiovascular than in the young. Ask about connective tissue disease; patients with Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome often dissect much younger, in their 30s, because of aortic root dilatation.
  • In suspected dissection, ask about symptoms of branch-vessel malperfusion: stroke symptoms, limb ischaemia, abdominal pain (mesenteric) and reduced urine output.

Remember the variations: dissection of the descending aorta may present with interscapular pain, dissection can produce myocardial infarction-like features (including ST elevation if a coronary ostium is involved), and some patients present with syncope alone.

Risk scoring

The Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score (ADD-RS) scores one point for each category present: high-risk conditions (Marfan or other connective tissue disease, family history of aortic disease, known aortic valve disease, recent aortic manipulation, known thoracic aneurysm); high-risk pain features (abrupt onset, severe, ripping or tearing); and high-risk examination features (pulse deficit or BP differential, focal neurological deficit with pain, new aortic regurgitation murmur with pain, hypotension or shock). Giuseppe scores at least 2, which is high probability: he goes straight to CT angiography and a D-dimer is not used to rule dissection out. In lower-probability patients the ESC guidance uses a negative D-dimer with a low ADD-RS to make dissection unlikely.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: he was white zone on arrival but already had a pulse deficit and 10/10 pain. His fall to yellow zone values with a concerned nurse means early shock: in type A dissection think tamponade from haemopericardium, rupture, acute aortic regurgitation or coronary involvement. Use the higher arm reading.
  • ECG: first-degree AV block (on verapamil) and long-standing LVH with strain, unchanged from 2024. No STEMI, but a normal or non-specific ECG does not exclude dissection.
  • Bloods: a markedly raised D-dimer is consistent with dissection, though at an ADD-RS of 2 or more it adds little; lactate and low Hb show hypoperfusion and possible blood loss; the mild troponin rise may be demand or coronary ostial involvement and is never a reason for antithrombotics. Coagulation and the group and screen prepare for theatre.
  • CT aortogram: the investigation of choice in the ED. It classifies the dissection, maps branch involvement and shows complications. Transthoracic echo at the bedside can show the flap, aortic regurgitation and a pericardial effusion, but a normal echo does not exclude dissection. A chest X-ray may show a widened mediastinum but is often normal.

Management

  • Type A is a surgical emergency. Call cardiothoracic surgery at once for emergency repair, with cardiac anaesthesia and ICU; mortality rises with every hour without surgery. Do not delay theatre for further imaging. In an unstable patient, bedside echo for tamponade should be immediate, and CTS may take him straight to theatre without waiting for CT.
  • Never give antithrombotics: aspirin, heparin and thrombolysis can be fatal. This is why dissection must be considered before treating any chest pain as ACS.
  • Resuscitate: two large-bore cannulas, crossmatch, the blood bank alerted, BP measured in the higher (left) arm, or by a left radial arterial line (the right under-reads because of brachiocephalic involvement), urinary catheter for output (with care in a man with previous retention).
  • If hypotensive: no BP-lowering drugs; give fluid or blood in small volumes to maintain perfusion. Tamponade from a type A dissection is treated by surgery; pericardiocentesis is not routine and is only considered as a bridge with the surgical team.
  • If hypertensive (anti-impulse therapy): IV beta blocker first (esmolol, metoprolol or labetalol), aiming for HR about 60 and systolic 100 to 120 mmHg, adding a vasodilator only after beta blockade to avoid reflex tachycardia. This is only for confirmed hypertension (arterial line) without tamponade physiology, and only with CTS/ICU or senior input; beta blockade is avoided while there is tamponade or hypotension, because the tachycardia is then compensatory and blocking it can precipitate collapse. Giuseppe takes verapamil and has first-degree AV block, so IV beta blockade also risks bradycardia and heart block and is titrated with ICU input.
  • Analgesia: titrated IV opioid, which also reduces the sympathetic drive.

Type B dissections (not involving the ascending aorta) are usually managed medically with anti-impulse therapy, with endovascular repair for complications such as malperfusion or rupture.

Differentials

Myocardial infarction is the most important mimic and the most dangerous mistake to make, because its treatment kills a patient with dissection. PE causes syncope and breathlessness but lacks the pulse deficit and murmur. Pneumothorax and pericarditis are argued against at the bedside and by the CT. Support every differential with positives and pertinent negatives from the history and examination.

Safety netting and follow-up

In hospital, safety netting means clear escalation triggers (falling BP, change in pain, new neurological signs, abdominal or leg pain, low urine output), a structured handover to cardiothoracic surgery and ICU, and telling Giuseppe and his wife what to report straight away. After repair the remaining dissected aorta needs lifelong imaging surveillance, strict BP control (ACC/AHA suggests below 130/80 mmHg) usually including a beta blocker, smoking cessation, cardiac rehabilitation and GP follow-up. Given his father's sudden death, aortic screening for first-degree relatives should be considered.
points: Sudden, maximal, tearing chest pain radiating to the back, especially with syncope, is aortic dissection until proven otherwise; descending dissection may give interscapular pain and some patients present with syncope alone.

At the bedside, compare both radial pulses and the BP in both arms, listen for aortic regurgitation and screen for neurological, abdominal and limb malperfusion. An ADD-RS of 2 or more means CT angiography without relying on D-dimer.
A normal or non-specific ECG does not exclude dissection, and dissection can mimic myocardial infarction. Never give aspirin, heparin or thrombolysis until dissection has been considered.

Stanford type A (ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency: call cardiothoracic surgery at once. Hypotension suggests tamponade, rupture or acute aortic regurgitation; resuscitate and go to theatre rather than lower the BP.

When hypertensive, anti-impulse therapy starts with an IV beta blocker, aiming for HR about 60 and systolic 100 to 120 mmHg, with a vasodilator only after beta blockade; avoid beta blockade while there is tamponade or hypotension, and beware heart block with verapamil.
Take risk factors seriously: hypertension, smoking, age, family history of sudden death or aortic disease, and connective tissue disorders (which cause dissection at a younger age).
